questions.stem: A 47-year-old man presented with an intensely painful ulcer of 13 days’ duration over the glans penis, surrounding the urethral orifice. The lesion had started as multiple small superficial ulcers, which had then coalesced. The ulcer had distinct raised thickened erythematous edges. There was necrotic slough and a foul-smelling hemopurulent discharge. The penis was edematous, and there was bilateral tender inguinal lymphadenopathy. He had had unprotected insertive and receptive anal sex with at least 20 men in the preceding 3 months. Investigations: HIV: Ag/Ab negative Syphilis: EIA negative Direct wet mount microscopy: trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Entamoeba histolytica Primary infection of the skin by Entamoeba histolytica can be acquired by direct contact with an infected subject during vaginal or anal intercourse. Identification of trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells is consistent with a clinical picture of amebic infection. Biopsy may be necessary to demonstrate trophozoites and to exclude other diagnoses such as squamous cell carcinoma. PCR may be useful in confirming the diagnosis. (Image from Assessments. In Cohen J, Powderly W , Opal S, eds. Infectious Diseases. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2017.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q49

questions.question: After 48 hours there was no growth on MacConkey agar and pinpoint growth on chocolate agar. Preliminary tests: oxidase negative, weakly catalase positive, and urease negative.
questions.question_raw: After 48 hours, there was no growth on MAC and pinpoint growth on the chocolate. Preliminary tests: ox -, weak cat +, and urease -.
questions.model_answer: Francisella tularensis. A tiny, fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus that grows only as pinpoint colonies on cysteine-enriched/chocolate agar, fails to grow on MacConkey, and is oxidase negative, weakly (or beta-lactamase-variably) catalase positive, and urease negative — distinguishing it from Haemophilus (oxidase/catalase positive, X and V dependent) and Brucella (urease positive).
questions.beyond_mandell: Francisella is not covered in the Haemophilus chapter; identification per Mandell Francisella tularensis chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Francisella tularensis, treat with cipro/gent (doxy/cipro for mild disease).

questions.question: [image-based question: Staphylococcus streak on blood agar plate shown with satelliting colonies] Name 3 genera of bacteria that show this satellitism characteristic.
questions.question_raw: [image-based question: Staph streak on BAP shown with satelliting colonies]

parts.text: Name 3 genera of bacteria that have this characteristic.

parts_raw.text: Name 3 genera of bacteria that have this characteristic.

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus (V-factor/NAD dependent, satellites around Staphylococcus which supplies V factor from lysed erythrocytes). (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Haemophilus/Actinobacillus spp., similar V-factor dependence). (3) Abiotrophia/Granulicatella (nutritionally variant streptococci).
questions.beyond_mandell: Abiotrophia/Granulicatella satellitism is established microbiology, not stated in this chapter.

questions.question: You isolate from both aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles a gram-negative pathogen that grows well on sheep blood agar and chocolate agar but fails to grow on MacConkey. List 2 organisms (from different genera) that meet all these characteristics.
questions.question_raw: 27. You isolate from both aerobic and anaerobic blood culture bottles a gram negative pathogen that grows well on sheep blood agar and chocolate agar, but fails to grow on MacConkey.

parts.text: List 2 organisms (from different genus) that meet all these characteristics.

parts_raw.text: List 2 organisms (from different genus) that meet all these characteristics.

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus influenzae — fastidious gram-negative coccobacillus growing on chocolate agar, not MacConkey; a HACEK organism. (2) Aggregatibacter aphrophilus — another fastidious HACEK gram-negative that grows on blood/chocolate but not MacConkey. (Other acceptable different-genus fastidious GNB not in this chapter include Pasteurella, Eikenella, Capnocytophaga, Brucella.)

cohort_answer.text: (fastidious Gram negs) Pasteurella multocida (gram- coccobacilli); Capnocytophaga canimorsus (gram- rod); Eikenella corrodens (gram- rod); Brucella; Bartonella; Francisella.

questions.question: Name two gram-negative bacteria that are seen in aerobic and anaerobic blood cultures and that grow on blood agar but not on MacConkey.

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus influenzae. (2) Aggregatibacter aphrophilus. Both are fastidious HACEK-group gram-negative organisms requiring enriched (chocolate/blood) media and failing on MacConkey. (Brucella and Pasteurella are also acceptable non-lactose-fermenting fastidious GNB.)

questions.question: Name five of the most common gram-negative organisms that cause infective endocarditis (genus only).
questions.question_raw: AM 24. Name 5 of the most common gram negative organisms that cause IE (genus only) (2.5)

parts.text: Name five of the most common gram-negative organisms that cause infective endocarditis.

parts_raw.text: Name 5 of the most common Gram negative organisms that cause IE

questions.model_answer: The HACEK group of fastidious gram-negative bacilli: (1) Haemophilus (e.g., H. parainfluenzae). (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus; A. actinomycetemcomitans, A. aphrophilus). (3) Cardiobacterium (C. hominis). (4) Eikenella (E. corrodens). (5) Kingella (K. kingae).

cohort_answer.text: Haemophilus spp.; Aggregatibacter spp. (Actinomycetemcomitans); Cardiobacterium hominis; Eikenella corrodens; Kingella kingae (HACEK group, all gram negative bacilli).

questions.question: Causes of gram-negative infective endocarditis.

parts.text: What are the 5 most common gram-negative causes of infective endocarditis?

parts_raw.text: What are the 5 most common gram (-) causes of infective endocarditis?

questions.model_answer: The classic gram-negative causes are the fastidious HACEK group (collectively ~1.7% of cases): (1) Haemophilus species; (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) actinomycetemcomitans; (3) Cardiobacterium hominis; (4) Eikenella corrodens; (5) Kingella species. Non-HACEK gram-negative bacilli (~2.1%) are led by Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

questions.question: Regarding culture-negative endocarditis, what are the 5 most common gram-negative causes of infective endocarditis?

parts.text: Culture-negative endocarditis - what are the 5 most common gram-negative causes of IE?

parts_raw.text: Culture negative endocarditis – what are the 5 most common gram negative causes of IE?

questions.model_answer: The HACEK group (fastidious gram-negative organisms, ~1.7% of definite IE): (1) Haemophilus species; (2) Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus) actinomycetemcomitans; (3) Cardiobacterium hominis; (4) Eikenella corrodens; (5) Kingella species.

cohort_answer.text: Last year's answer (assuming native valve, HACEK 2%): Haemophilus spp.; Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans; Cardiobacterium hominis; Eikinella corrodens; Kingella kingae. Non-HACEK GNB (2%): E coli; K pneumoniae. From IDSA/AHA guidelines: HACEK 5-10% of community acquired NVE in non-IVDU: Haemophilus species, Aggregatibacter species, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella species. Probably go with HACEK as the group for most common GNB IE causes

questions.question: A man who has sex with men with multiple partners presents with genital ulcers, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and fever. What is the diagnosis?
questions.question_raw: MSM with multiple partners presenting with genital ulcers, inguinal LAD, and fever.
questions.model_answer: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) — transient/painless genital ulcer followed by tender inguinal buboes and systemic features. Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) is the main alternative given painful ulcer plus fluctuant inguinal adenitis; herpes and primary syphilis should also be excluded.
questions.beyond_mandell: LGV specifics are in the Chlamydia trachomatis chapter; this chapter lists LGV only within the chancroid differential.

questions.question: A man who has sex with men with multiple partners presents with genital ulcers, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and fever. What is the causative organism?
questions.question_raw: MSM with multiple partners presenting with genital ulcers, inguinal LAD, and fever.
questions.model_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3.
questions.beyond_mandell: Per Mandell Chlamydia trachomatis chapter / CDC STI guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Chlamydia trachomatis serotypes L1, L2, L3

questions.question: A man who has sex with men with multiple partners presents with genital ulcers, inguinal lymphadenopathy, and fever. Give two possible treatments.
questions.question_raw: MSM with multiple partners presenting with genital ulcers, inguinal LAD, and fever.
questions.model_answer: (1) Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 21 days (first line). (2) Azithromycin 1 g PO once weekly x 3 weeks (alternative); erythromycin 500 mg PO QID x 21 days is the pregnancy option.
questions.beyond_mandell: LGV therapy per CDC STI treatment guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: First line: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x21 days. Second line: Azithromycin 1g PO once weekly for 3 weeks. Erythromycin 500mg PO QID x21 days (in pregnancy)

questions.question: For a list of sexually transmitted infections, state what investigations (if any) are indicated and the first-line treatment for each. Address a man who has sex with men presenting with painful inguinal lymphadenopathy.
questions.question_raw: List of various STIs - what investigations (if any) are indicated, and first line tx option for each?
questions.model_answer: Consider LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3). Investigations: NAAT for C. trachomatis with LGV-specific molecular testing on urine and rectal (+/- throat) specimens, and/or aspirate of a fluctuant lymph node; screen for concurrent HIV and other STIs. Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 21 days (alternative azithromycin) — aspirate fluctuant buboes rather than incise.
questions.beyond_mandell: LGV testing/therapy per CDC STI guidelines.

cohort_answer.text: Consider LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3). Request special testing for LGV from urine (+/- rectal, throat) +/- LN aspiration. Treatment: doxy or azithro x21 days

questions.question: State the preferred therapy for chancroid.
questions.model_answer: Azithromycin 1 g PO as a single dose is the CDC-recommended treatment. Alternatives: ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose, ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x 3 days, or erythromycin base 500 mg PO TID x 7 days; single-dose azithromycin or ceftriaxone are preferred for adherence. Response may be delayed with HIV coinfection.

cohort_answer.text: Cipro 500mg PO x1 OR Azithro 1g PO x1 OR Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1 - but increased failures in HIV. Chancroid = genital ulcer disease due to Haemophilus ducreyi, a fastidious Gram-negative rod

questions.question: Doxycycline in the treatment of genital ulcer disease.

parts.text: List 3 pathogens (genus and species) in which doxycycline can be considered for treatment for genital ulcers.

parts_raw.text: List 3 pathogens (genus and species) in which Doxycycline CAN be considered for treatment for genital ulcers.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Treponema pallidum — doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14 days is the standard alternative to benzathine penicillin G for primary/secondary syphilis. (2) Chlamydia trachomatis (serovars L1–L3, lymphogranuloma venereum) — tetracycline congeners are standard therapy, 14–21 days. (3) Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis/granuloma inguinale) — doxycycline is one of the effective agents, given for 3 weeks or until lesions heal.

questions.question: Genital ulcer disease and doxycycline therapy.
questions.question_raw: 8) 3 organisms genus and species causing genital ulcer disease that may be treated with doxy

parts.text: Name three organisms (genus and species) causing genital ulcer disease that may be treated with doxycycline.

parts_raw.text: 3 organisms genus and species causing genital ulcer disease that may be treated with doxy

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Treponema pallidum (syphilitic chancre) — doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14 days as penicillin alternative. (2) Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1–L3 (LGV) — tetracycline congener for 14–21 days. (3) Klebsiella granulomatis (donovanosis) — doxycycline for 3 weeks or until healed.

parts.text: 2 GNB that grow on blood and chocolate agar but not on MacConkey?

parts_raw.text: A) 2 GNB that grow on blood and chocolate agar but not on MAC?

questions.model_answer: (1) Haemophilus influenzae. (2) Aggregatibacter aphrophilus.
